description_full: Salesforce, Inc. provides customer relationship management technology services that connect companies and customers together in the United States, Europe, and the Asia Pacific. The company offers Agentforce, which enables customers to build, deploy, and manage enterprise-grade, autonomous AI agents at scale, enabling humans and agents to work together; Agentforce Sales, an integrated platform that brings together the power of humans with AI agents to help sales teams for selling, managing, and automating entire sales processes; Agentforce Service, which enables companies in every industry to bring all of their customer, employee, IT, and field service needs onto one integrated AI-powered platform; Data 360, a data engine that gives AI agents their context and serves as the foundation for how customers unify service offerings, making their data actionable for both humans and agents; Informatica, an AI-powered data management platform that enables customers to discover, integrate, govern, and deliver trusted data at scale across hybrid and multi-cloud environments; and Slack, a conversational interface for the agentic enterprise where people and agents work together, connecting knowledge, actions, and data in real time. It also provides marketing platforms; commerce services, which empower shopping experiences across various customer touchpoints; integration and analytics solutions; Salesforce Starter, a suite for small and medium-sized businesses that brings sales, service, marketing, and commerce together; and a field service solution that enables companies to connect service agents, dispatchers, and mobile employees through one centralized platform to schedule and dispatch work, as well as track and manage jobs. It serves financial services, healthcare and life sciences, manufacturing, automotive, and government sectors. Salesforce, Inc. was incorporated in 1999 and is headquartered in San Francisco, California.

Each employee generates $173K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $42K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 23× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (9/10).
financial_summary: Salesforce, Inc. is a large-cap technology business with a $175.8B market cap on $41.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +16% over the past three years and +23% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 2% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 75% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $14.4B in free cash flow — roughly 35 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.01× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 26× is fortress-like.
Management returns a meaningful 8.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 3.0% of the shares.

sect: Its 20% operating margin runs 13pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.86x).
It accounts for 0.9% of sector revenue and 0.8% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+53.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 5% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 19% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 21% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 47% and a beta of 1.27, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.67 vs 5y 1.37), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $2.3B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 36% in the 2020 crash, 50% in the 2022 bear market and 70% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 22% below its DCF fair value of $274, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 76%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $187 to $411 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 19.5 vs 26.7 and P/FCF 12.2 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 91% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 8.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 53 covering analysts target $287 on average, 34% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 2% falls short of the cost of capital of 10.5%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 5.81).
It runs a 75% gross margin and converts 35% of revenue into free cash flow, or 26% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 2.01x.
ROE of 13% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.9x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 15pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 14.4% of revenue on R&D and 8.5% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.5x net debt to EBITDA ($9.6B of cash against $14.4B of debt), with interest covered 25.7x.
The current ratio of 0.76 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
Goodwill makes up 52% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 16.2% over 3 years, 14.3% over 5 years and 22.7% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 28.6% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.37 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 1.7x annual revenue and deferred revenue up 28%.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (1.4% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 41, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 3.0%, and institutions hold 87%.
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 2 sales over the past year, net $173K sold.
It returns 8.1% a year to shareholders (7.2% in buybacks and 0.8% in dividends).
people: With about 83,334 employees, each generates about $498K of revenue, 1.3x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 24.1% a year.
That works out to $173K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $11.4M (23x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
